extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying point of view (first/second/third, free indirect, cinematic) in fiction, describing strengths/weaknesses, subtypes, and practical craft criteria (consistency, information control, voice, reliability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of POV
rubrics_metrics.description: POV is the perspective from which a story is told. It shapes intimacy, reliability, scope, and what readers can know.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Person
rubrics_metrics.description: "I", "me", "we"; includes first person protagonist and first person witness/observer (e.g., Nick Carraway, Watson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: intimacy, voice, unreliable narrator possibilities. Cons: limited to narrator's perceptions; can become claustrophobic; risk of "I" overuse. Consider whether the narrator's limited view and voice suit the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Person
rubrics_metrics.description: "You"; a rare POV often used in choose-your-own-adventure, lyrical, or experimental fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: implicates reader; creates strange intimacy. Cons: can feel gimmicky; sustaining length is hard. Use when you want to implicate the reader or create a disorienting intimacy, but beware of reader resistance over long stretches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person — Limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses he/she/they and is tied to one character's perceptions; the most common modern POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: combines outside view with deep character access. Cons: can drift toward telling. Use to get close to a character while retaining narrative distance; control drift into summary/telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person — Omniscient
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator knows all characters' thoughts and can comment or judge; common in 19th-century fiction (Tolstoy, Eliot, Dickens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: scope, author intervention, panoramic view. Cons: can feel old-fashioned; demands a strong narrator voice. Use for wide-ranging narratives that benefit from authorial commentary, but ensure the omniscient voice is strong and intentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Person — Objective / Cinematic
rubrics_metrics.description: External-only narration with no access to characters' thoughts (example: Hemingway's "Hills Like White Elephants").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: discipline; leaves space for reader inference. Cons: no interiority. Use when you want a restrained, show-not-tell approach that makes readers infer interior states from action and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free Indirect Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person prose colored by a character's thought language; pioneered by Austen and developed by Flaubert and Joyce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows fluid movement between narration and inner voice without quotation; useful for blending narrator perspective with character consciousness while retaining third-person grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make shifts deliberate and signalled (e.g., chapters, section breaks) so they read as intentional effects rather than errors. Uncontrolled shifting is jarring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability to story
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the POV give us what the story needs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the POV that provides the right intimacy, scope, and information access for the story's themes and plot needs rather than defaulting to a favored POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: No "head-hopping"
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid uncontrolled shifts mid-scene between characters' minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head-hopping (mid-scene shifts of focalization) confuses readers; keep a scene's focalization consistent or use clear breaks/techniques to change focalizer intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information control
rubrics_metrics.description: POV determines what readers know and when they know it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use POV deliberately to control revelations, suspense, and dramatic irony. The chosen perspective should align with how and when you want information revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice match
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's diction/register should fit the character or implied author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the narrator's voice (word choice, level of formality, idiom) aligns with character identity or the intended authorial stance; mismatched voice undermines credibility and immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear/intentional about whether the narrator can be trusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and signal whether the narrator is reliable or unreliable; intentional unreliability can be a device, but accidental ambiguity can frustrate readers.
